correctness.rationale: The closed-neighborhood local update reduces each shore exactly to one of four initial-pattern forms. Every comparison among time-varying counts is in a seven-label set. All 80 compatible linear extensions and 56 threshold-cut pairs were enumerated symbolically, including tie cases by linear extension; \(F^{6}=F^{4}\) and the stated iff condition for \(F^{5}\ne F^{3}\) hold for all 4,480 abstract cases. The last-layer formula is obtained by summing binomial weights over the proved inequalities. Independent labelled-vertex C++ evolution covered 2,632 graph-threshold instances and 4,884,036 initial strings; this finite check corroborates but does not establish the unbounded claim. The time-four trajectories were checked to enter opposite shore-consensus states.

originality.rationale: The full arXiv primary work of Kuhlman et al. establishes eventual period at most two for synchronous bi-threshold dynamics, but not a four-step universal cutoff, exact transient-four criterion, or binomial last-layer census for complete bipartite graphs. Its special graph examples concern principally asynchronous systems on trees. General majority, monotone threshold protocols and mod-two parity networks have different dynamics, so their results do not imply the theorem. Searches of publications, related indexed findings and accessible earlier theorem titles did not reveal an equivalent result; possible historical unindexed equivalence remains.

value.rationale: The infinite two-parameter family and unrestricted positive thresholds expose a sharp size-independent relaxation cutoff, with a necessary-and-sufficient graph-size imbalance obstruction and exact labelled last-transient population. These time-to-attractor and basin-size facts are not supplied by general eventual-period theorems. They explain precisely when two densely communicating communities have a delayed four-step transient and how many initial configurations produce it.
